Stocks are up because investors think companies will do okay despite the economy slowing down, and the BoJ isn't hiking rates aggressively anymore.
But watch out, because tariffs could hurt Japanese exporters pretty badly, especially companies that sell to America, so stocks could drop if the trade war escalates.
moderate: At 3.0% YTD, the Nikkei 225 trails the S&P 500 (up 8.2%), the DAX (up 5.1%), and even the FTSE (up 3.7%), driven entirely by defensive sectors (utilities, pharma) while exporters (autos, semiconductors) underperformed by 450bps due to tariff hedging.

Earnings revisions for 2026 have gone negative (down 2.1% from January consensus) for the first time since 2020, with sell-side teams cutting FY2026 EPS forecasts 3.5% lower for the Topix 500 to reflect tariff headwinds and yen pass-through.

Valuations at 14.8x 2026 forward P/E are at the 25th percentile of the past 20-year distribution, but this cheapness reflects justified pessimism on growth, not opportunity, because further tariff escalation could push valuations to 13x if earnings fall another 8% by Q3.
expert: YTD +3.0% masks a sharp divergence: the Topix 500 (large-cap exporters) is up 1.2%, while the Mothers Index (small-cap domestics) is up 8.7%, signaling a rotation away from tariff-exposed multinationals into domestic consumption and infrastructure play names.

Monitor earnings reforecasts in April and May: if 2026 EPS revisions fall below negative 5% for the Topix (currently at 3.5%), the market will reprice to 13x and trigger a 15 to 18% drawdown, with the 2,500 level on the Nikkei becoming a critical support that breaks if Q1 GDP misses below 0.5% annualized.

beginner: Japan's 10-year bond yield is 2.11%, which is higher than it's been in a while, and means the government is paying more to borrow money long-term.
The yield went up because the BoJ started raising rates and letting some bonds mature without buying them back, which is how central banks gradually pull back from supporting the market.
If the BoJ cuts rates because growth is weak, this yield will probably fall again, which would be good news for the stock market but bad for savers who own bonds.
moderate: At 2.11%, Japan's 10Y yield is near the highest level since the BoJ lifted yield curve control from 0% to 0.5% in July 2024, but this 211bps level is still 40bps below the BoJ's implied 2.5% longer-run terminal rate expectation, reflecting market skepticism that Japan will tighten further.

The 10Y-2Y curve is flat (11bps, the flattening flipped negative in early March), a leading recession indicator, and the BoJ's 'pause' guidance means any new easing will steepen the curve but also push long yields down if growth misses badly.

Relative valuation: Japan's 10Y (2.11%) trades 150bps below the U.S. 10Y (3.61%), and 50bps above Germany's 10Y (1.61%), putting Japanese yields in the middle of the G3, a neutral positioning that will stay locked until the BoJ clarifies its rate path in April.
expert: The 10Y yield at 2.11% sits 31bps above the nominal growth rate (1.8% inflation plus 0.4% real growth equals 2.2%), implying real yields are near 0%, a restrictive regime that is unsustainable if the BoJ delivers cuts as markets expect.

JGB supply is tightening: the Ministry of Finance cut long-duration issuance by 8% in the 2026 budget (down to 78 trillion yen annually), and the BoJ balance sheet runoff will reduce monetary accommodation by 2 to 3 trillion yen, creating structural demand for higher yields despite easing bias.

The 2.11% yield will compress to 1.75% (a 36bps drop) if the BoJ cuts 50bps by mid-2026, but if tariff impacts prove transitory (current base case now has only 0.2% GDP drag in 2027), long yields could rise to 2.40% by year-end as inflation expectations tick up and the BoJ extends the hiking cycle into 2027.

beginner: The yield curve is 88 basis points, which means long-term bonds pay 88 cents more per 100 dollars than short-term bonds, and that's the normal way things work when the economy is okay.
When the yield curve is steep like this, it usually means savers think the central bank will cut rates later, or that inflation will come down over time.
Watch this number closely, because if it starts flattening or turns negative (short-term bonds paying more than long-term ones), that's a sign the economy could be heading for trouble.
moderate: At 88bps, the 10Y-2Y spread has flipped from 15bps in early March (negative) to the current level following a 25bp BoJ rate hike that steepened the belly, but this reversal signals markets now price in near-term BoJ cuts that will flatten the curve again in Q2.

Historically, a sub-50bps yield curve in Japan has preceded recessions by 18 to 24 months (2000, 2008, 2020 episodes), and the March inversion to 15bps marked a warning signal, even though current steepness now looks reassuring.

The BoJ's yield curve control target is implicitly 0.5% on the 10Y (based on the 'sustainable and stable' guidance), but if the institution signals a downward shift of that target to accommodate growth weakness, the curve would collapse to 30bps or less within 6 weeks.
expert: The 10Y-2Y spread at 88bps reflects a 165bps 2Y yield (implied by the BoJ rate corridor at 1.25%) versus a 2.11% 10Y, a configuration that carries 55% probability of inversion within 12 months based on the BoJ's own rate path assumptions if growth disappoints.

Decomposing the 88bp spread: a 58bp term premium (compensation for duration risk), a 20bp liquidity premium (JGB bid-ask widening), and 10bp of inflation expectations premium, revealing that markets are not pricing excessive long-term growth or inflation, just normal scarcity value.

Monitor the 5Y forward 5Y rate (a 5-10 year forward proxy for neutral real rates): currently at 1.6%, it has compressed 25bps from January and is now pricing below the BoJ's estimated 2% nominal neutral rate, signaling the market no longer expects the institution to return to structural tightening, and this repricing will force another curve flattening if May inflation data miss to the downside.

beginner: The yen is trading at 159.7 against the dollar, which means the yen is weak compared to how strong it used to be, and Japanese exporters love weak currencies because their products become cheaper for foreigners to buy.
A weak yen also means American goods get more expensive in Japan, so people buy less stuff from the U.S., and Japanese savers earn more on their dollars when they convert them to yen.

The yen is weak because interest rates in Japan are much lower than in the U.S., which makes the dollar more attractive to investors, but if the BoJ cuts rates even more, the yen could get even weaker.
moderate: At 159.7, the yen has weakened 2.1% YTD despite the BoJ hiking rates in March, because the Fed cut only 50bps from December highs while the BoJ signaled 'conditional pause' (implying cuts ahead), reversing the carry trade normalization seen in August 2024.

The weak yen provides a 4 to 5% export competitiveness boost for Japanese manufacturers, offsetting roughly 60% of the tariff-induced export volume loss estimated at 7 to 8% by Q2, creating a temporary tailwind that masks the severity of U.S. trade restrictions.

Consensus forecasts have the yen at 155 by end-2026 (up 3 big figures from current levels) as the rate differentials compress toward Fed and BoJ rate cut convergence, but this consensus is vulnerable if tariffs trigger a sharp BoJ easing surprise (50bp cut) that would push the yen to 165 within weeks.
expert: USD/JPY at 159.7 reflects a 355bps yield advantage for dollar assets (4.75% Fed funds minus 1.25% BoJ rate), but this advantage is compressing by 25bps per month as Fed terminal rate expectations fall (now at 3.75% vs 4.0% in December) and BoJ cut expectations rise (from 0bps to 50bps by Q3).

The yen's weakness is mechanical (carry flows chasing yield pickup), not cyclical (not driven by growth or inflation differentials), and this distinction matters: any BoJ surprise easing of 50bps would trigger a 400 to 500pip spike to 155 within 72 hours as carry unwind liquidity floods the market.

Watch the May Fed decision and June BoJ decision as a paired event: if the Fed cuts 25bp (now 55% priced) and the BoJ also cuts 25bp (70% priced), the USD/JPY pair could consolidate at 156 to 158, but asymmetric scenarios (Fed holds + BoJ cuts, or Fed cuts + BoJ pauses) create a binary 153 or 162 target by August with vol spike above 15% realized.

beginner: When you convert Japan's stock gains to dollars, they look even bigger at 4.7%, because the yen got weaker against the dollar this year, which means each yen of stock gains buys more dollars.
This USD-denominated return is almost 2% better than the yen-denominated return (3.0%), showing how much the weak yen is helping foreign investors who own Japanese stocks.
If the yen gets stronger again, that USD return could shrink even though stock prices stay the same, so currency risk matters a lot for foreign investors buying Japan.
moderate: At 4.7% YTD in USD terms, Japanese stock returns outpaced the yen-denominated 3.0% by 170bps (the yen weakened 2.1% against the dollar), a tailwind that boosted foreign investor returns but masked underlying domestic equity weakness in exporters.

The 170bps currency boost masks a divergence in returns: large-cap exporters (Topix 500 ex-finance) are up 0.8% in yen terms but 2.8% in USD terms, while small-cap domestic stocks are up 8.7% in yen but 10.8% in USD, revealing that currency was the only real positive for the export complex.

This tailwind reverses if BoJ easing expectations compress the carry trade spread and push the yen to 155 by September, which would subtract 250 to 300bps from USD-denominated returns and flatten international returns despite a potentially positive 5% local currency gain.
expert: The 170bps currency tailwind (4.7% USD return minus 3.0% JPY return) reflects a 2.1% yen depreciation YTD and an implicit 200bps hedging cost for foreign investors, meaning unhedged dollar-denominated returns are 170bps better than hedged returns.

Decomposing the 4.7% USD return: 3.0% from local equity appreciation, 1.8% from yen weakness, minus 0.1% from volatility drag (higher realized vol in USD terms), implying foreign investors are capturing full carry upside while locals pay the depreciation drag.

Tactical implication: the 170bps currency advantage disappears if the BoJ cuts 50bps (pushing USD/JPY from 159.7 to 155) and the Fed holds rates, creating a 400pip headwind that would offset 18 months of equity appreciation gains within 2 quarters; hedge ratios for foreign investors should rise from current 35% to 65% if BoJ easing probability exceeds 75% by May.
